set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A survival study compared two treatments for a lymphoma. Patients given treatment A were mostly enrolled at diagnosis, while patients given treatment B were mostly enrolled after earlier therapy had failed. Treatment A showed far better survival. Which bias could falsely create this difference?
opts: Migration bias
Migration bias arises when patients drop out of a study or change groups during it, whereas these groups differed when they entered.
Susceptibility bias
Correct, because the groups assembled for the study differ in their point in the disease course and in prior treatment, which alone can change survival.
Measurement bias
Measurement bias means one group's outcome is more likely to be detected than the other's, whereas the problem here is who was enrolled in each group.
Publication bias
Publication bias concerns whether studies without statistically significant results get published, not differences between the patients within one study.
set1.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 22, 23, 24; 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Recall components of a PICO question
set1.q: An abstract reads: "We randomly assigned 600 adults with acute low back pain seen in primary care to naproxen or acetaminophen and measured disability scores at four weeks." Which detail is the outcome element of a matching clinical question?
opts: Disability at four weeks
Correct, because the outcome is what the clinician hopes to measure, improve or affect, here disability scores at four weeks.
Adults with acute low back pain
Adults with acute low back pain in primary care are the patients, the group whose care the question concerns.
Naproxen
Naproxen is one of the two treatments being compared, the intervention or its comparison, not the result that was measured.
Acetaminophen
Acetaminophen is the other treatment in the comparison, not the result that was measured.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 9

set1.io: Identify components of a journal article
set1.q: A rural clinician reading an abstract wants to know whether the study's participants and setting resemble her own patients before reading further. Which question of a cursory review is she asking?
opts: Is it likely to be true?
Asking whether a study is likely to be true directs the reader to its design, not to its patients and setting.
To whom does it apply?
Correct, because asking to whom the study applies directs the reader to the patients and setting, one step of a cursory review.
What was concluded?
Asking what was concluded directs the reader to the conclusions rather than to who was studied.
How big was the effect?
Asking how big the effect was belongs to the in-depth review and is answered by the figures and tables.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 38, 41

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A cohort study found that adults with gray hair had twice the rate of heart attack of adults without it. Gray hair was far more common in the older participants, and older age also raises the risk of heart attack. Which term best describes age in this study?
opts: An effect modifier
An effect modifier is a variable whose presence or absence changes the effect of an exposure and is not a bias, whereas age here creates the apparent link itself.
The dependent variable
The dependent variable is the possible effect, which in this study is heart attack rather than age.
The independent variable
The independent variable is the possible cause under study, which in this study is gray hair rather than age.
A confounding variable
Correct, because age is associated with both the exposure (gray hair) and the outcome (heart attack), so its effect cannot be separated from the effect of gray hair.
set1.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 37, 42; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 26, 28

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: During an outbreak, 200 people in a city of 100,000 were diagnosed with a new respiratory illness, and 10 of those 200 died of it. What is the case-fatality ratio?
opts: 0.01 percent
That divides the 10 deaths by the whole city of 100,000, a death rate for the population rather than the proportion of diagnosed people who died.
0.2 percent
That is the share of the city diagnosed with the illness, 200 of 100,000, which describes how many were affected rather than how many of them died.
5 percent
Correct, because the case-fatality ratio is the number of people who die divided by the number of people who have the disease: 10/200 = 5 percent.
95 percent
That is the proportion of diagnosed people who survived, whereas the case-fatality ratio counts those who die, and framing by deaths or by survivors needs care.
set1.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 16; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A study of a home exercise program for heart failure enrolled volunteers who answered an advertisement placed in fitness centers. The comparison group was taken from a list of patients recently discharged from the hospital. The exercise group had fewer readmissions over a year. Which threat to validity is most likely?
opts: Measurement bias
Measurement bias comes from a method of measurement that gives incorrect results, while the problem here lies in how the two groups were chosen.
Attrition effect
The attrition effect arises when participants drop out of a study, and nothing here says anyone left either group.
Performance bias
Performance bias is a difference in the care given to the two groups other than the topic of interest, while these groups differed before the program began.
Selection bias
Correct, because the groups differ in more ways that affect the outcome than only the program, so few conclusions can be drawn about the program itself.
set1.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 40, 41, 44, 45

set1.io: Formulate PICO question
set1.q: A clinician wonders whether vitamin D helps older people avoid falls. Which question is best formed for searching the literature?
opts: In adults over 70, does vitamin D, compared with placebo, reduce falls?
Correct, because it names all four parts: the patients (adults over 70), the intervention (vitamin D), the comparison (placebo) and the outcome (falls).
In adults over 70, does daily vitamin D taken every winter reduce falls?
It names the patients, the intervention and the outcome, but no comparison, the main alternative to weigh against vitamin D.
Does daily vitamin D, compared with a placebo tablet, reduce falls?
It names the intervention, the comparison and the outcome, but no patients, so it does not describe a group similar to the clinician's.
In adults over 70, is daily vitamin D better than a placebo tablet?
It names the patients, the intervention and the comparison, but "better" names no outcome to measure.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 9, 10

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: In a randomized trial of surgery versus medication, the coordinator enrolling patients could see the next assignment on an open list. Several frail patients were held back until a medication slot came up. Which safeguard was missing?
opts: Allocation concealment
Correct, because allocation concealment means the researchers assigning patients to treatment groups are blinded, so the coordinator could not have known the next assignment.
A placebo control
A placebo is indistinguishable from the treatment and helps blinding of participants, but it would not hide the list from the coordinator.
Stratified sampling
Stratified sampling creates subgroups to represent how groups exist in the population, which does not hide upcoming assignments.
Exclusion criteria
Exclusion criteria are factors that prevent inclusion in a study, and holding frail patients back for one arm is not a stated criterion.
set1.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 15, 18, 21, 23

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A hospital team identified 120 adults admitted with a first hip fracture and 240 adults of similar age admitted for planned surgery who had no fracture. Interviewers then asked everyone in both groups about long-term use of a sleeping medication during the previous five years. Which study design did the team use?
opts: Retrospective cohort study
A retrospective cohort is defined by exposure from past records and followed forward to the present for the outcome, whereas these groups were chosen by outcome first.
Case-control study
Correct, because the groups were defined by the outcome (fracture or no fracture) and then assessed for a difference in past exposure, with the controls drawn from the hospital.
Prospective cohort study
A prospective cohort is assembled in the present on the basis of exposure and followed forward, whereas this study started from people who already had the outcome.
Cross-sectional study
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at the same time in one population, whereas here fracture cases and controls were selected separately before exposure was asked about.
set1.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 17, 22, 27, 28; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A trial of an inhaled drug for chronic lung disease reports relative risks, drug versus placebo, with 95 percent confidence intervals: hospital admission 0.70 (0.55 to 0.90), death 0.85 (0.60 to 1.20), pneumonia 1.40 (0.90 to 2.20), and oral thrush 2.10 (1.40 to 3.10). Which outcome shows a statistically significant increase with the drug?
opts: Pneumonia
Its point estimate of 1.40 suggests more pneumonia, but the interval of 0.90 to 2.20 includes 1, the value of no association.
Oral thrush
Correct, because its whole interval lies above 1, the null value at which risk is equal in the two groups, so a true relative risk of 1 is not within the interval.
Death
Its interval of 0.60 to 1.20 includes 1, the value of no association, so a true difference in deaths is not shown either way.
Hospital admission
Its interval lies wholly below 1, which shows a significant decrease in admissions with the drug, not an increase.
set1.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 14, 15; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 20

set1.io: Evaluate information in selected resources
set1.q: A clinician looking into a treatment finds three sources: a case series of 12 patients, a cohort study of 5,000 patients, and a systematic review of eight randomized controlled trials. Which source sits highest in the hierarchy of evidence?
opts: The cohort study
Cohort studies sit below randomized controlled trials on the pyramid, so 5,000 patients do not lift a cohort above a review of trials.
The case series
Case series sit below cohort and case-control studies on the pyramid, so a detailed account of 12 patients ranks lowest of the three.
The systematic review
Correct, because systematic reviews sit at the top of the clinical studies pyramid, and studies at higher levels are least vulnerable to bias and more generalizable.
They rank equally
All studies serve a purpose and can guide practice, but some designs are stronger than others, which is why evidence is ranked as a hierarchy.
set1.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8; 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 33, 34, 35

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: Two drugs were tested for stroke prevention over five years. For drug A, the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke was 40, and the number needed to harm (major bleeding) was 25. For drug B, the number needed to treat was 120, and the number needed to harm was 400. Which statement best describes the two drugs?
opts: B prevents more strokes and harms less often
B does harm less often, with its larger number needed to harm, but its larger number needed to treat means it is the less effective drug.
A prevents more strokes and harms less often
A does prevent more strokes, but its number needed to harm of 25 is far smaller than B's 400, so harm comes after fewer patients are treated.
B prevents more strokes but harms more often
B's number needed to treat of 120 is larger than A's 40, so B is less effective, and its larger number needed to harm means it harms less.
A prevents more strokes but harms more often
Correct, because a smaller number needed to treat means a more effective intervention, while a smaller number needed to harm means harm occurs after fewer patients are treated.

mis.B prevents more strokes and harms less o: larger number needed to treat read as better
mis.A prevents more strokes and harms less o: smaller number needed to harm read as safer

set1.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 13, 14

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A cohort study followed 400 adults who worked night shifts and 400 who worked only day shifts for five years. A peptic ulcer developed in 24 of the night-shift workers and 8 of the day-shift workers. What is the relative risk of ulcer for night-shift work?
opts: That is the attributable risk, the incidence in exposed persons (0.06) minus the incidence in non-exposed persons (0.02), not their ratio.
That divides the day-shift incidence by the night-shift incidence, which inverts the ratio, since relative risk puts the exposed group's incidence on top.
Correct, because relative risk is the incidence in exposed persons divided by the incidence in non-exposed persons: 24/400 = 0.06 and 8/400 = 0.02, and 0.06/0.02 = 3.
That is the incidence among night-shift workers expressed as a percentage (24 of 400 is 6 percent), not a comparison with the day-shift workers.

mis.0.04: attributable risk confused with relative risk

set1.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 17, 18, 19, 24

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A study of a knee examination maneuver for a torn ligament reports a sensitivity of 80 percent and a specificity of 90 percent. What is the positive likelihood ratio of the maneuver?
opts: That is the negative likelihood ratio, (1 - sensitivity)/specificity = 0.2/0.9, which applies to a negative result.
That divides sensitivity by specificity, 0.8/0.9, but the denominator of the positive likelihood ratio is 1 - specificity.
That divides specificity by 1 - sensitivity, 0.9/0.2, which puts the wrong property in both the numerator and the denominator.
Correct, because the positive likelihood ratio is sensitivity/(1 - specificity) = 0.8/0.1 = 8, moderate evidence to rule the tear in.
set1.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 30, 31, 44

set1.io: Evaluate information in selected resources
set1.q: A health website about a joint supplement is written by a board-certified physician, gives detailed information on dosing and side effects, and was updated last month. The site is owned by the company that sells the supplement. Which element of the ABCD (Author, Bias, Content, Date) method raises the main concern?
opts: Bias
Correct, because a site owned by the seller of the product it describes raises the question of bias, which the author's credentials, the detail and the recent date do not answer.
Author
The author element asks about credentials, qualifications and expertise in the field, and a board-certified physician meets it.
Content
The content element concerns the level of detail, and this site gives detailed dosing and side-effect information.
Date
The date element asks whether the source is still current, and an update last month meets it.
set1.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 17, 18

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A randomized trial of a migraine drug reports 1.5 fewer migraine days per month than placebo, with a p value of 0.08. How should this result be described?
opts: Significant at the 0.05 level
A result is generally accepted as significant when p is less than 0.05, and 0.08 is above that value.
Highly significant
Highly significant is generally used for a p value of 0.01, a 1 in 100 probability of chance, which is far below 0.08.
Not statistically significant
Correct, because p values less than 0.05 are generally accepted as statistically significant, and 0.08 is above that cutoff.
Proof that the drug has no effect
A result that is not significant can be a type II error, a false negative that study limitations can cause, so it does not prove there is no effect.

mis.Highly significant: any reported p value is significant
mis.Proof that the drug has no effect: absence of significance proves no effect

set1.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 7, 11

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: Researchers compared each country's yearly sales of sugar-sweetened drinks per person with its rate of type 2 diabetes across 40 countries, using only national totals. No data on any individual person were collected. Countries with higher sales had higher diabetes rates. Which study design is this?
opts: Meta-analysis
A meta-analysis pools data from multiple studies to produce a single large study, whereas here national totals were compared rather than the results of separate studies.
Case-control study
A case-control study compares individuals with and without a disease for exposure, but this study used no data on any individual person.
Ecologic study
Correct, because a cross-sectional ecologic study relates the frequency of a characteristic to an outcome using population-level data, so applying its result to one person risks the ecologic fallacy.
Cohort study
A cohort study follows a group of people over time on the basis of exposure, whereas here whole countries were compared using population totals.
set1.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 18, 19, 22, 25, 32

set1.io: Recall components of a PICO question
set1.q: A pediatrician asks: "In children with an ear infection, does a delayed antibiotic prescription, compared with an immediate antibiotic, relieve ear pain as well within three days?" Which part of the question is the outcome?
opts: Children with an ear infection
Children with an ear infection are the patients or population, the group of patients the question describes.
Relief of ear pain within three days
Correct, because the outcome is what the clinician hopes to accomplish, measure, improve or affect, here relief of ear pain within three days.
A delayed antibiotic prescription
The delayed prescription is the intervention, the main option being considered.
An immediate antibiotic
The immediate antibiotic is the comparison, the main alternative weighed against the intervention.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 9

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: An experienced cardiologist writes an overview of heart failure care, covering diagnosis, drugs, devices and end-of-life planning. She cites the trials she considers most useful, and the article describes no search method or rules for choosing studies. Which kind of article is this?
opts: Systematic review
A systematic review answers a specific, predetermined question with explicit criteria for selecting studies, and this broad overview has neither.
Meta-analysis
A meta-analysis combines the numerical results of similar studies into a weighted estimate of effect, and this overview pools nothing.
Narrative review
Correct, because it is an expert summary of evidence covering a broad topic and a range of issues, and its unstructured choice of cited articles is a recognized disadvantage.
Cohort study
A cohort study is primary research that follows a group of people over time, whereas this article summarizes trials that others carried out.

mis.Systematic review: any review of trials is systematic

set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 4, 5, 6, 22; 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 3, 25

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A company sponsored five trials of its new pain drug. The two trials that found a statistically significant benefit were published, while the three that found no significant difference were never submitted to a journal. A later review of the published trials concluded that the drug works. Which bias most affected that review?
opts: Publication bias
Correct, because research without statistically significant results is less likely to be published, and a sponsor is less likely to support research that is unfavorable to its product.
Selection bias
Selection bias arises when a study's comparison groups differ in more than the factor studied, whereas the distortion here lies in which whole trials reached print.
Non-response bias
Non-response bias arises when people who answer a survey differ from those who do not, a problem inside one study rather than across the literature.
Confounding
Confounding is a covariate associated with both exposure and outcome within a study, and it cannot explain why the trials without significant results went unpublished.
set1.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 40, 42, 44, 46

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A cohort study of 20,000 adults found that bladder cancer rates rose step by step with the number of cigarettes smoked per day, from light to moderate to heavy smokers. Which criterion for causality does this finding support?
opts: Temporality
Temporality means the cause precedes the effect, whereas this finding concerns how the rate changes with the amount smoked.
Reversibility
Reversibility means decreased exposure leads to less disease, which would need people who cut down or quit, not a comparison of amounts smoked.
Dose-response
Correct, because a larger exposure leading to a higher rate of disease is the dose-response criterion for causality.
Consistency
Consistency means findings are replicable in other studies, whereas this is a single study.
set1.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: On January 1, a survey of a retirement community of 2,000 residents found 160 with diabetes. Over the following year, 40 residents who had not had diabetes developed it. What was the prevalence of diabetes on January 1?
opts: 2 percent
That uses the 40 new cases arising during the year, which describe incidence (new cases in previously healthy people), not who had the condition on January 1.
8 percent
Correct, because prevalence is the portion of a group with a condition at a specific point in time: 160 of 2,000 residents is 8 percent.
10 percent
That counts the 160 existing cases plus the 40 new ones, which gives the prevalence at the end of the year rather than on January 1.
20 percent
That divides the 40 new cases by the 200 total cases, while prevalence divides the existing cases by the whole community of 2,000.
set1.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 15, 17, 20

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A blood test for a liver disease was given to 1,000 adults, and a biopsy, the gold standard, showed that 50 of them had the disease. The test was positive in 40 of the 50 with the disease and in 95 of the 950 without it. An adult in this study tests positive. What is the probability that this adult has the disease?
opts: 30 percent
Correct, because this is the positive predictive value, true positives divided by all positives: 40/(40 + 95) = 30 percent.
80 percent
That is the sensitivity, 40 of the 50 diseased adults testing positive, which starts from disease rather than from a positive result.
90 percent
That is the specificity, 855 of the 950 adults without the disease testing negative.
99 percent
That is the negative predictive value, 855 true negatives out of 865 negative tests, which applies to a negative result.

mis.99 percent: negative predictive value used for a positive result

set1.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 16, 19, 24, 25

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A trial of a new inhaler was run in ordinary primary care clinics, with patients managing their own doses, usual reminders and no extra monitoring, to learn how well it works in everyday practice. What does this trial mainly measure?
opts: Efficacy
Efficacy represents ideal trial circumstances, such as close monitoring, which this trial deliberately avoided.
Non-inferiority
A non-inferiority trial asks whether a new treatment is unlikely to be less effective than an established one, which is not the aim stated here.
Effectiveness
Correct, because effectiveness represents real, ordinary circumstances and takes into account compliance, practicality and cost.
Allocation concealment
Allocation concealment means the researchers assigning patients to treatment groups are blinded, a safeguard rather than something a trial measures.
set1.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 23, 27, 28, 29

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A randomized trial tests whether a supervised exercise and education program, started after a first heart attack, reduces later complications such as heart failure. Which level of prevention does the trial study?
opts: Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention detects disease while it is still asymptomatic, as screening does, whereas these patients have already had a heart attack.
Primary prevention
Primary prevention removes underlying causes or risk factors to prevent a disease from occurring, but this disease has already occurred.
Chemoprevention
Chemoprevention is one of the types of preventive care, listed with immunization, screening and counseling, not one of the three levels of prevention.
Tertiary prevention
Correct, because tertiary prevention is clinical intervention to reduce complications following a diagnosis, and its treatments are usually studied with randomized trials.

mis.Secondary prevention: any prevention after risk is secondary

set1.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 4, 5, 12

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A trial of 40 patients followed for three months found no statistically significant difference in relapse between a new drug and placebo. A later trial of 2,000 patients followed for two years found a clear benefit of the same drug. What error did the first trial most likely make?
opts: A type I error
A type I error is a false positive, concluding that a relationship exists when it does not, which is the opposite of the first trial's finding.
Recall bias
Recall bias comes from participants' difficulty remembering, whereas relapse in a trial is an outcome the researchers observe.
Confounding
Confounding is a third factor that distorts an exposure-outcome relationship, not the name for a study failing to detect a difference that exists.
A type II error
Correct, because concluding that no relationship exists when one does is a type II error, a false negative that can result from study limitations such as the length of follow-up.
set1.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 9, 10, 11, 34

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A team wants to learn whether a medication taken during pregnancy raises the risk of a rare childhood cancer, diagnosed in about 1 in 50,000 children. Its budget covers a study of a few hundred children, and an answer is needed within about a year. Which study design best fits these limits?
opts: Case-control study
Correct, because it starts from children who already have the cancer, so it needs smaller samples and no waiting for the condition to develop.
Prospective cohort study
A cohort must enroll a large group, is expensive, and gives results only after many years, and because so many more subjects are needed than develop the disease, it is poorly suited to rare diseases.
Randomized controlled trial
Experimental studies of risk in humans are limited by ethical constraints, so pregnant women cannot be assigned to a possibly harmful medication.
Cross-sectional study
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and disease at one time and is poor for determining cause and effect, so it suits developing hypotheses rather than testing this one.

mis.Cross-sectional study: cheap and quick suits any aim

set1.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 15, 16, 29; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

set1.io: Discuss the relevance of journal articles to clinical practice
set1.q: A randomized trial of a heart failure drug enrolled only men aged 40 to 60 with normal kidney function, at three academic medical centers, and found a clear benefit. A clinician in a community practice wants to give the drug to an 82-year-old woman with kidney disease. Which property of the trial is most in question for her?
opts: Its internal validity
Internal validity is the degree to which the results are correct for the sample of patients studied, and nothing here suggests they were wrong for those men.
Its statistical significance
Statistical significance concerns how likely a result is to have happened by chance, not whether it applies to a patient unlike those studied.
Its reliability
Reliability is consistency of measurement on repeated attempts, which does not address whether the trial's patients resemble hers.
Its external validity
Correct, because external validity is the degree to which results are also true in other clinical settings, and this sample may not represent her.
set1.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 50, 51; 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 6; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 58

set1.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set1.q: A health department mailed a survey about exercise habits to 5,000 randomly chosen residents. Only 900 returned it, and most of those who replied were retired adults with more free time. The department reported that residents exercised far more than expected. Which threat to validity is most likely?
opts: Attrition effect
The attrition effect is participants dropping out of a study after entering it, whereas most residents here never took part at all.
Non-response bias
Correct, because the people who responded differ from those who did not, so the results may not reflect the whole population.
Measurement bias
Measurement bias is a method of measurement that leads to incorrect results, whereas the problem here is who replied, not how exercise was measured.
Confounding
Confounding needs a covariate associated with both an exposure and an outcome, whereas this survey describes one group's habits without testing an exposure.

mis.Attrition effect: not answering confused with dropping out

set1.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 41, 42, 44

set1.io: Identify components of a journal article
set1.q: After reading an abstract, a reader wants to check how participants were assigned to groups and whether the outcome assessors were blinded. Which part of the article answers these questions?
opts: The introduction
The introduction shows the importance of the research question, not how the study was carried out.
The methods
Correct, because how strong the methods were is answered in the methods section during an in-depth review.
The discussion
The discussion places the study in context rather than describing how participants were assigned and assessed.
The figures and tables
The figures and tables show how big the effect was, not how the study was designed.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 39, 41

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: Using factory employment records from 1990, investigators identified 800 workers who had handled an industrial solvent and 800 who had not. They then searched medical records from 1990 up to the present for new cases of kidney disease in each group. Which study design is this?
opts: Prospective cohort study
A prospective cohort is assembled in the present and followed into the future, whereas these workers' exposures and outcomes had already occurred and were found in records.
Retrospective cohort study
Correct, because the investigators went back in history to define the groups by exposure and followed the members forward to the present to find the outcome.
Case-control study
A case-control study selects people by outcome (kidney disease or not) and then looks at exposure, whereas these groups were chosen by solvent exposure.
Cross-sectional study
A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at a single point in time, whereas this study followed each group through more than 30 years of records.
set2.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 17, 22, 27, 28; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 12

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A research group wants to measure how often stroke, dementia and hip fracture newly develop in older adults who do and do not use a common sleep medication. Funding allows the group to follow participants for 15 years. Which study design fits this aim?
opts: Case-control study
A case-control study starts from people with one condition and controls without it, and its measure is the odds ratio, so it does not establish incidence directly.
Cross-sectional study
A cross-sectional study is a snapshot of who has a condition at one point in time, which gives prevalence rather than how often new cases arise.
Prospective cohort study
Correct, because a cohort establishes incidence directly and can assess the relationship between one exposure and a number of outcomes.
Case series
A case series is descriptive, describing the characteristics of one group of people, so it offers no comparison of users with nonusers.

set2.io: Recall components of a PICO question
set2.q: A clinician asks: "In adults over 65 with type 2 diabetes, does adding a daily walking program, compared with diet advice alone, lower average blood glucose after six months?" In this clinical question, which part is the comparison?
opts: A daily walking program
The walking program is the intervention, the main option being considered, while the comparison is what it is weighed against.
Adults over 65 with type 2 diabetes
Adults over 65 with type 2 diabetes are the patients or population, the group similar to the clinician's own patients.
Lower average blood glucose
Lower average blood glucose is the outcome, what the clinician hopes to accomplish, measure, improve or affect.
Diet advice alone
Correct, because the comparison is the main alternative to compare with the intervention, here diet advice given without the walking program.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 9, 10

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: In a trial of a new antidepressant, a pharmacist prepared identical-looking capsules of drug and placebo. Neither the participants nor the researchers who assessed them knew who received which. Which term describes this trial?
opts: Single-blind
In a single-blind trial the subjects are unaware but the researchers are aware, whereas here the researchers were unaware as well.
Open label
Open label means no blinding is done, whereas identical capsules kept everyone here unaware.
Double-blind
Correct, because in a double-blind trial the researchers and the subjects are both unaware of which treatment is being received.
Non-inferiority
A non-inferiority trial is defined by its aim, showing a new treatment is unlikely to be less effective, not by who is unaware of the treatment.
set2.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 21, 23, 29

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A trial of 30,000 adults found that a new blood pressure drug lowered systolic pressure by 1 millimeter of mercury more than the standard drug, with a p value below 0.001. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: Clinically important, because p is so small
A very small p value shows the difference is unlikely to be due to chance, but statistical significance does not imply clinical significance.
Not significant, because the difference is small
Small differences can still be statistically significant, and a p value of 0.001 is generally accepted as very highly significant.
Probably due to chance, given the small difference
A p value of 0.001 means the probability of chance is 1 in 1,000, so chance is an unlikely explanation.
Significant, but perhaps not clinically important
Correct, because statistical significance does not imply clinical significance, and a difference can have a very small p value yet no relevance to clinical practice.
set2.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 7, 22

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A meta-analysis of a lifestyle program reports a relative risk of 0.80 (95 percent confidence interval 0.70 to 0.92) for developing type 2 diabetes and 0.95 (0.80 to 1.12) for heart attack. Which statement is correct?
opts: Only the heart attack result is significant
The heart attack interval includes 1, the null value at which risk is equal in both groups, so that result is not statistically significant.
Both results are statistically significant
Both point estimates are below 1, but the heart attack interval of 0.80 to 1.12 still includes 1, so only one result is significant.
Only the diabetes result is significant
Correct, because the diabetes interval lies entirely below 1, while the heart attack interval runs from 0.80 to 1.12 and so includes 1, the value of no association.
Neither result is statistically significant
The diabetes interval of 0.70 to 0.92 stays below 1, so the true value is not likely to be 1 and that result is statistically significant.
set2.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 14, 15; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A 12-month trial of a weight-loss drug enrolled 300 adults. By month 12, 40 percent of the drug group and 10 percent of the placebo group had stopped attending visits, many after reporting nausea. Only those who completed the trial were analyzed. Which threat to validity is most prominent?
opts: Attrition effect
Correct, because participants dropping out reduces the sample size, and a trial must account for withdrawals and dropouts so that attrition does not falsely skew the outcome data.
Non-response bias
Non-response bias arises when people who answer a survey differ from those who do not, whereas these participants enrolled and then left a trial partway through.
Procedural bias
Procedural bias arises when the method of delivering an interview or questionnaire affects the results, which is not what happened here.
Publication bias
Publication bias concerns which studies reach print, with research lacking significant results less likely to be published, not who stays in a trial.
set2.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 44, 46; 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 27, 30

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A rapid urine test for bladder infection was compared with urine culture, the gold standard, in 400 patients. Culture was positive in 100 of them. The rapid test was positive in 90 of those 100 and in 15 of the 300 patients with a negative culture. What is the sensitivity of the rapid test?
opts: 86 percent
That is the positive predictive value, 90 true positives out of the 105 positive tests, which starts from a positive result rather than from infection.
90 percent
Correct, because sensitivity is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives: 90/(90 + 10) = 90 percent.
95 percent
That is the specificity, 285 true negatives out of the 300 patients without infection.
97 percent
That is the negative predictive value, 285 true negatives out of the 295 negative tests.
set2.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 16, 19, 24

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A trial compared a dietary supplement with placebo on 25 different outcomes. Only one, hair thickness, reached a p value of 0.04. The published article was built around that finding and did not say how many outcomes had been examined or which had been primary. What is the main problem with its conclusion?
opts: Multiple comparisons
Correct, because selecting the more interesting comparisons after the analysis, without saying how many questions were examined or which was primary, can distort the data.
A type II error
A type II error is a false negative, concluding that no relationship exists when one does, whereas this article claims a positive finding.
Recall bias
Recall bias arises from participants' difficulty remembering, whereas this trial measured its outcomes directly.
Confounding
Confounding is a third factor that distorts a relationship, whereas the problem here is how the one significant result was chosen.
set2.cite: 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 11, 17, 18, 34

set2.io: Recall components of a PICO question
set2.q: A student drafts this question for a literature search: "In adult smokers, does a nicotine patch help people stay smoke-free for one year?" Which element of a PICO (Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes) question is missing?
opts: Comparison
Correct, because nothing in the question states the main alternative to compare with the nicotine patch, such as no patch.
Patients
Adult smokers are named as the patients, the group of people the question is about.
Intervention
The nicotine patch is named as the intervention, the main option being considered.
Outcomes
Staying smoke-free for one year is named as the outcome, the result the student hopes to measure.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 9, 16

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A case-control study enrolled 80 patients with liver cancer and 160 controls without it. Forty of the cases and 20 of the controls had a history of a particular viral infection. What is the odds ratio for the infection?
opts: That is the odds of infection among the controls, 20 infected to 140 uninfected, which is only the denominator of the odds ratio.
That is the odds of infection among the cases alone, 40 infected to 40 uninfected, before it is compared with the controls' odds.
That divides the proportion of cases infected (40 of 80) by the proportion of controls infected (20 of 160), a ratio of proportions rather than of odds.
Correct, because the odds of exposure are 40/40 = 1 in cases and 20/140 in controls, and their ratio, ad/bc = (40 x 140)/(20 x 40), is 7.

mis.4: relative risk method used on case-control data

set2.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 35, 36, 37, 38

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A new oral antibiotic costs less and causes fewer side effects than an established injected antibiotic. A trial is designed to show only that the new drug is unlikely to be less effective than the established one. Which type of trial is this?
opts: Superiority trial
A superiority trial determines whether one treatment is better than another, a stronger claim than this trial sets out to make.
Phase I trial
A phase I trial uses a small number of participants, with no control group, to identify a safe or tolerated dose.
Trial of N = 1
A trial of N = 1 gives one patient one treatment at a time, with patient and provider blinded, rather than comparing two groups.
Non-inferiority trial
Correct, because a non-inferiority trial determines whether a new treatment, which may be cheaper, safer or easier, is unlikely to be less effective than an established one.
set2.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 29, 32, 33

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: In a case-control study of a birth defect, mothers of affected infants and mothers of healthy infants were interviewed a year after delivery about the medicines they had taken during pregnancy. No pharmacy or medical records were checked. Which bias most threatens the exposure data?
opts: Selection bias
Selection bias concerns how people get into a study, whereas the weak point named here is how exposure was learned once they were in it.
Confounding
Confounding is a third factor that distorts the relationship between exposure and outcome, whereas the problem here is the accuracy of the exposure information itself.
Recall bias
Correct, because the exposure was asked about rather than measured, so it depends on how well each mother remembers, and remembering is difficult.
Random error
Random error occurs by chance and is accounted for through the p values used in a study, whereas relying on memory for exposure is a named bias.
set2.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 33; 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A study tested a new automatic blood pressure cuff against an intra-arterial line, which shows the true pressure. Repeated cuff readings on the same patient agreed within 1 point of each other, but every reading was about 15 points higher than the true pressure. How should the cuff be described?
opts: Valid but not reliable
Validity means measuring what is supposed to be measured, and these readings were consistently 15 points off, while their close agreement shows reliability.
Both valid and reliable
Close agreement between repeated readings shows reliability, but a consistent 15-point error means the cuff does not measure what it is supposed to.
Neither valid nor reliable
Repeated readings that agree closely are the definition of reliability, so the cuff cannot be called unreliable.
Reliable but not valid
Correct, because repeated readings were consistent (reliability, or precision) but did not measure the true value (validity, or accuracy).
set2.cite: 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 52, 58, 59

set2.io: Recall components of a PICO question
set2.q: A researcher asks: "In working women, is regular night-shift work, compared with day work only, associated with a higher risk of breast cancer?" Which element is regular night-shift work?
opts: Patients, as the population
The patients or population here are working women, the group the question describes.
Intervention, as an exposure
Correct, because the intervention element can be an intervention, a prognostic factor or an exposure, and night-shift work is the exposure being considered.
Comparison, as the alternative
The comparison is day work only, the main alternative weighed against night-shift work.
Outcome, as the result measured
The outcome is the risk of breast cancer, what the researcher hopes to measure.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: In a 6-month weight-loss trial, the intervention group was weighed on a calibrated clinic scale at every visit. The control group reported weights from their own home scales, which were never checked. The trial reported more weight loss in the intervention group. Which threat to validity does this raise?
opts: Measurement bias
Correct, because the method of measurement differed between the groups and may lead to incorrect results, and calibrating measuring devices is how the validity of a measurement is ensured.
Selection bias
Selection bias arises when the groups are assembled so that they differ in more than the focus of the study, whereas the flaw here is in how weight was measured.
Non-response bias
Non-response bias arises when those who answer a survey differ from those who do not, and every participant here supplied a weight.
Reporting bias
Reporting bias means only a subset of the relevant data is made available, whereas here the data are complete but were measured differently.
set2.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 40, 41, 44, 45; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 52

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A survival study of patients after a heart attack used Cox proportional hazards regression, adjusted for age and sex. Patients with a ventricular arrhythmia had a hazard ratio for death of 3.0 compared with patients without one. How should this hazard ratio be read?
opts: One third the risk of dying
A hazard ratio below 1 is considered protective, but a hazard ratio of 3.0 is above 1, so the risk is higher, not lower.
A 3 percent risk of dying
A hazard ratio compares the risk of the outcome in two groups and is not itself a percentage of patients who die.
Survival three years shorter
A hazard ratio is interpreted as a relative risk of the outcome, not as a difference in survival time measured in years.
Three times the risk of dying
Correct, because a hazard ratio can be interpreted as a relative risk, so a value of 3 means the group with the factor has three times the risk of the outcome.
set2.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: In an unblinded trial of a new sleep medication against placebo, participants knew which pill they were taking. Many in the placebo group began using over-the-counter sleep aids during the study, and the drug showed little advantage. Which bias does this describe?
opts: Selection bias
Selection bias arises from how the groups were formed, so that they differ at the start, whereas these groups diverged in the care they received after assignment.
Performance bias
Correct, because care other than the topic of interest differed between the groups, and blinding study participants is what protects against it.
Non-response bias
Non-response bias arises when survey responders differ from non-respondents, whereas this describes extra treatment taken during a trial.
Reporting bias
Reporting bias means only a subset of the data is made available, whereas the problem here arose before any results were reported.
set2.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 40, 44, 45

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A published trial of a new arthritis drug listed six outcomes in its plan, including pain, function and stomach bleeding. The journal article reported only the two outcomes that favored the drug, and the other four were never made available. Which bias does this describe?
opts: Reporting bias
Correct, because only a subset of all the relevant data was made available, even though the trial itself was published.
Publication bias
Publication bias concerns research that never gets published, often because it lacks statistically significant results, whereas this trial did reach print.
Measurement bias
Measurement bias arises when the method of measurement leads to incorrect results, whereas the problem here is which results were shown.
Attrition effect
The attrition effect is participants dropping out and reducing the sample size, which nothing here describes.

mis.Publication bias: any missing results are publication bias

set2.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 41, 44, 45, 46

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: Four hundred adults with knee osteoarthritis were placed by a computer-generated random sequence either in a supervised exercise program or in usual care. Pain scores were measured in both groups after 12 weeks. What feature makes this study experimental rather than observational?
opts: The groups were followed forward in time
A cohort is also a group followed over time, and a cohort is observational, so following groups forward cannot be what makes this study experimental.
The investigators assigned the intervention
Correct, because in an experimental design the intervention (independent variable) is assigned and manipulated by the investigator, whereas in an observational design it is only observed.
Two groups were compared on an outcome
Comparing two or more groups makes a design analytic, and cohort and case-control studies do this too while remaining observational.
Pain was recorded as a numerical score
Numerical, measurable data mark quantitative research, which also includes cohort and case-control studies, so a score does not make a study experimental.
set2.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 6, 8, 9, 25

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A study of two blood tests for appendicitis reports that test A has a sensitivity of 98 percent and a specificity of 70 percent, while test B has a sensitivity of 75 percent and a specificity of 97 percent. A clinician wants a negative result to rule appendicitis out. Which choice is best?
opts: Test B, as high specificity leaves few false negatives
High specificity means very few false positives, not false negatives, so test B's lower sensitivity makes its negative result the less reassuring one.
Test A, as high sensitivity leaves few false negatives
Correct, because a negative result on a highly sensitive test rules disease out: when sensitivity is high, there are very few false negatives.
Test B, as a positive result on it rules disease in
A positive result on a highly specific test does rule disease in, but the clinician here wants a negative result that rules it out.
Test A, as high sensitivity leaves few false positives
High sensitivity means very few false negatives, while it is high specificity that means few false positives, so this reason is reversed.
set2.cite: 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: Identify components of a journal article
set2.q: A clinician scanning a list of new articles finds one whose title matches her question. She wants to learn quickly what the study was about and what it concluded. Which part of the article should she read first?
opts: The methods
The methods show how strong the research was, an in-depth question that comes after the abstract has shown the article is relevant.
The abstract
Correct, because a quick reading starts with the abstract, which shows what the study is about and what was concluded.
The discussion
The discussion gives context and belongs to the in-depth review, after the abstract has shown the article is worth reading.
The figures and tables
The figures and tables show how big the effect was, an in-depth question that comes after the abstract.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 38, 39, 40, 41

set2.io: Identify components of a journal article
set2.q: A reader has decided an article is relevant and now wants to see the actual size of the difference in outcomes between the groups, with the numbers for each group. Where should the reader look?
opts: The figures and tables
Correct, because the question of how big the effect was is answered by the figures and tables during an in-depth review.
The introduction
The introduction shows how important the research question is, not how large the effect was.
The methods
The methods show how strong the study's methods were, not the size of the effect it found.
The title
The title tells what the study is about, the first step of a cursory review, and gives no numbers.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 39, 41

set2.io: Evaluate information in selected resources
set2.q: A national task force reviews a screening test for adults over 85 and concludes, with moderate certainty, that the service has no net benefit. Which grade of recommendation does this conclusion match?
opts: Grade B
Grade B recommends the service, with high certainty of moderate net benefit or moderate certainty of moderate to substantial net benefit.
Grade C
Grade C means offering the service selectively, with at least moderate certainty that the net benefit is small rather than absent.
Grade D
Correct, because grade D recommends against a service when there is moderate or high certainty that it has no net benefit or that the harms outweigh the benefits.
Grade I
Grade I means the evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms, whereas this conclusion was reached with moderate certainty.

mis.Grade I: no benefit confused with insufficient evidence

set2.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Evidence MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 12, 13

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: Investigators followed 3,000 adults for ten years, comparing those who took a daily aspirin with those who did not, and counted the new cases of colon cancer in each group. Which measure of association should they report?
opts: Odds ratio
The odds ratio is the measure of association for case-control studies, which start from cases and controls rather than following a group forward.
Likelihood ratio
A likelihood ratio describes how much a test result changes the probability that a patient has a condition, so it belongs to studies of tests.
Case-fatality ratio
The case-fatality ratio is the number of people who die of a disease divided by the number who have it, which does not compare exposed and unexposed groups.
Relative risk
Correct, because a cohort study can directly calculate the incidence of disease in the exposed and the non-exposed, so relative risk is used rather than the odds ratio.
set2.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 35, 40; 4 PAJ5512 Tests MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: Investigators planning a study of a dietary supplement debate how to control confounding. One suggests matching participants on age and sex, and another suggests random assignment to supplement or placebo. Which advantage does random assignment offer over matching?
opts: It makes the results generalizable
Generalizability is often limited because study patients may not represent other populations, and randomization does not change who is enrolled.
It can be applied after data are collected
Randomization assigns participants before outcomes occur, so it cannot be applied after the data are collected.
It removes the need to blind anyone
Randomization decides who receives which treatment, while blinding keeps participants and researchers unaware of it, so one does not replace the other.
It balances factors no one chose to measure
Correct, because randomization is the only method of dealing with differences between groups whose benefits are not limited to the factors selected for consideration.
set2.cite: 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 25, 26; 7 PAJ5512 Risk MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 27; 8 PAJ5512 Research and Trials MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: An observational study reports that patients whose colon cancer was found by screening lived a median of 7 years after diagnosis, compared with 4 years for patients diagnosed after symptoms appeared. The tumors in both groups had similar growth rates, and patients in both groups died at about the same age. Which bias best explains the longer survival after diagnosis?
opts: Length-time bias
Length-time bias arises when screening detects more slow-developing conditions with better prognoses, but the tumors here grew at similar rates.
Lead-time bias
Correct, because screening moved the diagnosis earlier without moving the death, so the apparent gain is increased time knowing the diagnosis rather than improved survival.
Compliance bias
Compliance bias arises when screened people do better because they are more invested in their health, yet death came at about the same age in both groups.
Overdiagnosis
Overdiagnosis is finding a disease whose detection does not help the patient, an extreme example of length-time bias, which the similar growth rates rule out here.
set2.cite: 8 PAJ5512 Prevention MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 17, 18, 19, 21, 23

set2.io: Discuss the relevance of journal articles to clinical practice
set2.q: A trial at one referral hospital randomized patients, blinded the outcome assessors, kept the groups similar at baseline and followed every patient to the end. All participants were referred by specialists and had severe disease. Which description best fits the trial?
opts: Low internal, high external validity
Randomization, blinding and complete follow-up protect internal validity, and a referred, severe sample makes generalizability uncertain rather than high.
Low internal, uncertain external validity
The trial's methods protect the correctness of results for the sample studied, so its internal validity is high rather than low.
High internal, uncertain external validity
Correct, because its methods protect the correctness of the results for the patients studied, but referred patients with severe disease may not represent those in other clinical settings.
High internal and high external validity
Generalizability is rarely determined from a single study, and patients referred to one center may not represent other settings.

mis.Low internal, uncertain external validit: a single center means low internal validity

set2.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 51; 7 PAJ5512 Prognosis MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 26, 30

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A survey of 3,000 adults asked, in one interview, about current depression and about exercise in the past week. Adults with depression reported less exercise. The authors conclude that inactivity causes depression. What is the main weakness of that conclusion?
opts: It cannot measure how common depression is
Measuring the portion of a group with a condition at one point in time is exactly what a cross-sectional, or prevalence, study does well.
It cannot include adults without depression
Prevalence is measured by counting the number with and without the condition in the population, so adults without depression are counted too.
It cannot show which came first in time
Correct, because a cross-sectional study measures the risk factor and the condition at the same time, while causality requires that the cause precede the effect.
It cannot use questionnaires to collect data
Surveys and questionnaires are useful for collecting prevalence information, as in cross-sectional studies of food allergy.
set2.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 17; 3 PAJ5512 Rates and Measurement MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 15, 22, 23; 9 PAJ5512 Statistics Causation MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

set2.io: Interpret information presented in journal articles
set2.q: A county health department mailed one questionnaire to 2,400 randomly chosen adults during a single month. It asked whether each person currently smoked and whether each currently had a chronic cough, and both answers came from the same reply. No one was contacted again. Which study design is this?
opts: Cross-sectional study
Correct, because the data were obtained at a single point in time, with the risk factor (smoking) and the condition (cough) measured at the same time in each person.
Prospective cohort study
A prospective cohort assembles groups on the basis of exposure, collects baseline data and follows them over time, but no one here was followed after the single questionnaire.
Case-control study
A case-control study first defines groups by outcome (disease or no disease) and then assesses exposure, but these adults were sampled without regard to whether they had a cough.
Randomized controlled trial
In a randomized controlled trial the investigator randomly assigns subjects to treatment and control groups, but nothing was assigned here and smoking was only observed.
set2.cite: 2 PAJ5512 Study Design and Research Methods MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slides 9, 17, 22, 27, 30
